output.headline: Four men convicted as abuse survivor calls for change in consent law
output.bodyHtml:
Four men were convicted on Thursday of raping and sexually assaulting a woman who had been drugged by her husband, as she said the case raised “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”.

The Crown Prosecution Service said it was the first time a jury had convicted multiple defendants relating to organised drug-facilitated sexual assault in England.

It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice on how to approach their inquiries from investigators who worked on the case of Gisèle Pelicot – who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France – as comparisons have been drawn between the two cases.

In a statement outside court, Joanne Young – whose bravery was praised by the judge – said the convictions meant “that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system”.

Saying that she now lives “with a pain that’s hard to put into words”, she added: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed.

“At no point did anyone ask me for my consent. I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”

Joanne said she hoped the verdict would give other victims of abuse the confidence to come forward, even though the abuse had had a devastating impact on her life and the lives of her children.

“The court has today shown that there will be consequences for those who make the choice to abuse,” she said. “I’m determined that their choices will not define me, and I will now use my experience to try to help others. I also owe it to myself to live the best life I can with my children and loved ones as we move forward.”

Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, is the former wife of the former Conservative councillor, who pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against her.

Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

On Thursday, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial.

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor from Swindon, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration; Wilkins, a taxi driver from Swindon, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape; Macksoni, a former DJ and waste management worker from Bedfordshire, was convicted of rape; and Hassan, also from Swindon, was found guilty of sexual assault.

A further defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, from Somerset, had admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.

Mr Justice Saini refused bail applications for the four men convicted on Thursday, telling them they all faced “significant custodial sentences”.

All of the men, including Young and Hamilton, will be sentenced on 21 and 22 December at Winchester crown court.

After the verdicts, Wiltshire police said that although rare, the true scale of drug-facilitated sexual offences in the UK could be significantly underreported.

A spokesperson for Wiltshire police, which investigated Young’s offending, said other victims in similar cases may not know they had been targeted.

He added: “While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly underreported crime type.

“Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging.”

Young, a father of three, pleaded guilty in January to a total of 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife. He also admitted three charges of making indecent images of children, one of possessing prohibited images of children in July 2024 and four counts of possessing an extreme pornographic image between January 2019 and January 2024.

Over more than a decade, Young – who served as a Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 – drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

Prosecutors told the court the case was about whether it was ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first.

Sanderson-Doyle responded to an online advert in 2015 and visited the couple’s home in June 2016. Young filmed him sexually assaulting Joanne as she was drugged, blindfolded and restrained, and heard saying “No”.

Police identified Wilkins through distinctive tattoos shown in footage of his arrest, after he went to the home in July 2016 and was filmed by Young abusing Joanne, who was again blindfolded, restrained and seemingly asleep, without her consent being obtained.

Messages and digital evidence showed Young arranged for Hassan to visit, and that Hassan had sexual contact with her while she believed he was her husband; Macksoni visited and raped Joanne in February 2017, while Hassan sexually assaulted her in February 2023.

Speaking after the verdicts, James Foster, a specialist prosecutor at the CPS, said: “These men chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.

“By building the case with a suspect-centric approach, we could prove to a jury that Philip Young could not provide consent on the victim’s behalf and each defendant played a part in this horrific sexual abuse.

“During the trial, Macksoni, Wilkins, Sanderson-Doyle and Hassan hid behind the claim that they believed she was freely entering into a sexual relationship with them, despite never seeking reassurances that this was in fact the case.”
output.standfirst: Joanne Young says the convictions of four men mean other victims are more likely to come forward, after her husband drugged and raped her and invited strangers to abuse her for more than a decade.
output.progress: The four men will be sentenced in December, and Wiltshire police say such crimes may be significantly underreported.

output.headline: Youth mobility deal clears the way for a UK-EU reset
output.bodyHtml:
British and European negotiators moved within reach of a reset deal on Thursday night, provisionally agreeing to let 100,000 EU citizens come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

The EU dropped its demand that EU students attending British universities pay home tuition fees, it is understood, a last-minute concession made to get the deal over the line.

The UK had strongly resisted the EU text on the table, which would have committed it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but negotiators hammered out a compromise before 10pm, agreeing a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.

EU sources said both sides were on track for an agreement on Friday, as talks continued into the night.

The talks went “down to the wire”, sources said, as both sides worked through disagreements over the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules.

But on the eve of the summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.

France also appeared to compromise, after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.

The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards, but France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start.

Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, though the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.

Earlier on Thursday, the UK agreed to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in the new youth mobility scheme, accepting a cap of 100,000, instead of the 50,000 to 80,000 it had previously sought.

It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.

The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.

Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”

A spokesperson for the British prime minister said the talks were close, adding that if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4 per cent to British GDP, including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.

The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Related: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”

According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.

An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”

Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.

A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.

In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.

“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.

The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.

The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.

The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.

The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.

Related: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.

“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement on language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.

Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.

“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”
output.standfirst: The EU has dropped its demand for UK students to pay home tuition fees and agreed a 100,000 cap on youth mobility, though food and farming talks went down to the wire before Friday's summit.
output.progress: Negotiators are working through the night on food and farming terms, aiming to sign three agreements, including the food deal, on Friday.

output.headline: Government presses Google to take down Russell Brand’s prison message
output.bodyHtml:
A continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is examining whether Russell Brand broke prison rules meant to prevent ‘serious distress’ to the victims of crime, after Andy Burnham called on Google to take down Brand’s statement from YouTube.

The prison authorities are also considering whether Brand harassed his victims by issuing the comments through his wife, in which he insisted he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.

Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the ‘notoriety’ of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement.

Ministers asked for the video to be removed, but it has remained on YouTube days later; in it, Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, reads out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty.

Related: New law ‘may be needed’ after Google rejects call to remove Russell Brand’s YouTube prison message

Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he ‘wouldn’t leap’ to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: ‘I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.

‘You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.’

According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that ‘serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.’

The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast ‘must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence’.

It is understood that the inquiry is taking into account the right of prisoners to protest their innocence. However, there is a strict protocol governing the way such statements are issued and whether permission has been sought beforehand.

It is understood that there has been no proposal to move Brand, who is held in the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, to a higher-category prison, and he is likely to remain there, a specialist prison for sex offenders.

That is despite recent reports which claimed Brand was likely to be moved to a category A or B prison instead, after he protested his innocence.

The government has been in ‘dialogue’ with Google, YouTube’s owner, though it has no power to compel the company to remove the video.

‘We trust that they will do the right thing,’ a Downing Street spokesperson said when asked about the standoff. They said: ‘The prime minister’s position on this is that Russell Brand’s victims deserve peace, and we’ve heard enough from him.

‘We’ve asked YouTube to remove the content. I would also just point out that they acted before when they suspended Brand’s account from making money. Given he has been convicted of rape by a jury of his peers, we trust that they will act again.’

No 10 was repeatedly asked whether Burnham would personally welcome the video being removed, as well as Brand’s YouTube channel being disabled. It told reporters: ‘Removal ultimately depends on YouTube and the platform’s terms and conditions.’

A spokesperson for Google said: ‘We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.’

Kemi Badenoch said if she was in power she would not immediately demand Google remove the video.

The Conservative leader told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: ‘My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes.

‘I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that.’

• Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
output.standfirst: No 10 has asked YouTube to remove Russell Brand’s prison message, as the Ministry of Justice considers whether the rapist broke rules meant to protect victims from serious distress.
output.progress: The Ministry of Justice is investigating whether Brand broke prison rules, while No 10 presses Google to remove the video.

context.text: A justice minister met Google representatives to ask it to deactivate Brand’s YouTube account, after Meta had already disabled his Instagram and Facebook profiles, Sky News reported.

output.headline: Anthropic completes the biggest IPO in history, valuing it near $1.3tn
output.bodyHtml:
Anthropic closed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17 per cent higher than its initial public offering price. Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 at the close of market on Thursday, valuing the company at nearly $1.3tn, or $1.75tn on a fully diluted basis.

Anthropic’s shares, which soared 34 per cent to value the company at more than $2tn when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, closed above their $83 IPO price even after easing back from that early high of $111.50. The flotation ranked among the biggest in stock market history, and made the artificial intelligence startup, founded in 2021, one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world.

‘Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,’ said Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, who rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Anthropic announced late on Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters, an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June.

US stocks slumped at the end of trading, a potential sign that Anthropic’s record IPO alone was not enough to ease wider concerns over the AI industry’s volatility. Most of the major chipmakers’ stock prices closed the day lower than they started: Nvidia posted its sixth day of losses after its latest earnings call, while Micron and Broadcom also saw their share prices decline.

Related: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?

The company’s listing serves as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom, as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry are watching closely how it fares on the public market.

Anthropic’s stock market debut makes it the first firm focused entirely on AI ‘uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business’ to be publicly traded, analysts at Yorkville Ives said.

‘Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,’ Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a memo.

The company has seen explosive growth in revenue every year of its existence – sometimes more than 1,000 per cent – according to its investor prospectus, filed at the end of October. Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in revenue in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn for all of 2025.

‘You’ve seen an astronomical growth rate in terms of the top line,’ said Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm. ‘The question investors are going to be looking at leading up to the IPO, and once it’s public, is what happens to that growth rate.’

Anthropic is investing heavily to secure more compute – the processing and computational power provided by arrays of semiconductor chips, often housed in datacentres, that powers generative artificial intelligence and is the company’s single largest expense, about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026 – and expects its costs to balloon as a result. The company has also lost an enormous amount of money: it reported losses of $80bn in the first half of 2026, though that was largely due to a one-off charge, and losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of the year.

‘The development of frontier AI models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars,’ the company’s executives wrote in the prospectus.

Related: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick

Amodei has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models, after employees expressed concerns that the companies were building them irresponsibly, and Anthropic has disclosed in detail the ways its AI models may pose a danger to humanity – including being used to develop bioweapons or deepen repression around the world.

Anthropic beat competitors such as OpenAI to a listing on the US stock market, though the flotation comes amid uncertainty as the industry braces for any further fallout from the recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Schlossman said there is ‘huge volatility in the market’, and investors will be watching how sustainable the company’s AI growth proves to be. They are also keen to see how important Anthropic becomes within the wider AI ecosystem. The company has focused mainly on enterprise customers rather than individual consumers, and its Claude Code product has proved popular with software engineers.
output.standfirst: Anthropic’s shares closed at just over $97, valuing it near $1.3tn after the biggest IPO in history, though the stock eased from its early high as losses reached $104bn over nine months.
output.progress: Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown on developing the most advanced AI models, and Anthropic has disclosed in detail the risks they pose.

output.headline: Xi, Putin and Trump agree peace declaration at historic three-way summit
output.bodyHtml:
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement at an unprecedented trilateral summit, though the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included UN reform, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

Related: ‘Really making history’: five takeaways from the meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Related: ‘End your war, end it now’: Anthony Albanese tells Vladimir Putin to put a stop to Ukraine war

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times” on AI, a topic that was watched for but lacked detailed findings.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.
output.standfirst: Xi, Putin and Trump reached agreement at an unprecedented trilateral summit on priorities including UN reform and boosting oil supplies, though the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
output.progress: China, Russia and the US have committed to strategic stability and boosting oil supplies, with Xi calling for nuclear weapons to be eliminated over time.

output.headline: Letby’s lawyer applies to watchdog for court of appeal review
output.bodyHtml:
Lucy Letby’s lawyer has said the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns.

Letby’s lawyer Mark McDonald, who has applied to the miscarriages of justice watchdog, the Criminal Cases Review Commission, for Letby’s convictions to be referred back to the court of appeal, said: “These revelations about Prof Hindmarsh, and the failure to disclose material information about him to the defence at trial, raise fundamental questions, and it is more urgent than ever that the court of appeal re-examines the safety of all Lucy Letby’s convictions.

“She is an innocent woman in prison, serving whole-life sentences, yet material information that could have been of critical importance to her defence was not disclosed. Did the police know? How did this information remain undisclosed?

“We need answers. Lucy deserves answers. She should not have to spend another day behind bars while these fundamental questions remain unanswered.”

The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin.

The jury in the case were never told of the restriction placed on Hindmarsh, who was described by the prosecution in court as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

Two senior lawyers said serious concerns about an expert’s professional abilities, and non-disclosure to the defence, could be grounds for an appeal against convictions.

Letby’s defence lawyers were never told that Hindmarsh had been excluded from clinical practice, nor of an April 2023 tribunal ruling imposing a restriction. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has also said it was not informed.

Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Hindmarsh’s opinion that two babies were poisoned with insulin, for which Letby was found guilty of attempted murder, was considered crucial to Letby being convicted. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical and scientific experts have contributed to reports submitted with her CCRC application, arguing that the prosecution’s medical case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong.

This week a Guardian investigation revealed that while the trial was going on, Hindmarsh’s employer barred him from clinical practice, and reported to the General Medical Council (GMC), which was already investigating him, that it believed he posed a risk to the safety of child patients.

Hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin – at University College London hospitals trust (UCLH) when the trial began. He had also been an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital.

In March 2023, while the trial was continuing at Manchester crown court, Dr Tim Hodgson, a medical director at UCLH, wrote to the GMC: “On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Prof [Hindmarsh] to practise clinically even under supervision … I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Prof Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”

Hodgson set out safety concerns, including two cases in which he said Hindmarsh had advised child patients to stop taking insulin. The GMC then applied for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended, which Hindmarsh opposed. His barrister argued it would be disproportionate, and would impede his ability to work as an expert witness in legal cases.

On 21 April 2023, a medical practitioners tribunal declined to suspend Hindmarsh but ordered that he must be directly supervised in his clinical work. That appears to have had no practical effect because UCLH had barred him from treating patients at all.

Hindmarsh did tell Cheshire constabulary, which instructed him in the case, about the GMC investigation in December 2022, and the CPS informed Letby’s defence team, but said it would oppose the jury being told. The jury was never informed that the GMC had launched an investigation into concerns about Hindmarsh, referred by UCLH and Great Ormond Street. His contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated in July 2022, and the jury was not told about that either.

Nick Johnson KC, the lead prosecution barrister, described Hindmarsh to the jury on 23 February 2023 as “the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field” of insulin.

Letby’s defence team was not informed about the further developments of March and April 2023, including that Hindmarsh had been excluded from clinical practice; and the jury was never told.

McDonald said: “It is staggering that Hindmarsh was presented as the pre-eminent expert on insulin at the trial, gave crucial evidence alleging babies were poisoned with insulin – which many eminent experts say was wrong – and it was never disclosed that he was considered by his own hospital [to be] unsafe to treat children with insulin, and barred from clinical practice.”

A representative of Hindmarsh declined to answer questions from the Guardian, including whether he had failed to disclose the March and April developments to Cheshire constabulary. The police force declined to comment. The CPS confirmed it was never given the information.

The criminal procedure rules require expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them anything, including disciplinary proceedings, “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. The rules were introduced in 2014 after recommendations by the Law Commission to improve expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice.

The commission was set up after a series of notorious miscarriages of justice based partly on flawed evidence from medical expert witnesses. The cases included Sally Clark, a solicitor who was wrongly convicted in 1999 of killing her two infant sons.

Clark’s convictions were overturned in 2003 after a CCRC referral to the court of appeal, principally because key medical evidence had not been disclosed to the defence. A striking statistical opinion presented by an expert witness for the prosecution, about the likelihood of both sons dying, was also shown to be catastrophically wrong. Clark had spent more than three years in prison condemned as a child killer and never recovered from her ordeal; she died in 2007 of acute alcohol poisoning.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, said of the rules: “If there was a failure to make relevant disclosure of material undermining an expert’s opinion evidence, and where that opinion evidence was relevant to the central issues before the jury, then that failure could form part of the grounds of appeal. It all depends upon the facts of a particular case and potential weight of the non-disclosure upon the jury’s verdict.”

Pete Weatherby KC, a barrister with extensive experience of criminal trials, said: “The expert witness disclosure rules are there to protect the integrity of the trial process and avoid miscarriages of justice. Expert evidence was pivotal in the Lucy Letby prosecution because there was no direct or forensic evidence that she committed any of the criminal acts of which she was accused.

“Serious concerns about an expert’s conduct or judgment may be highly relevant to assessing their expertise, credibility, and the reliability of their evidence. If those concerns were not before the jury, that could be very significant for an appeal. If the full details were not obtained by the prosecution, and disclosed to the defence at the time, that would be even more significant.”

output.headline: Police arrest man in Bradford councillor Ibrar Ali case
output.bodyHtml:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford, which politicians have described as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”.

A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg.

A 32-year-old man fled to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue but was brought down some time later and arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

He remains in custody.

Officers were called just after 11am to reports that a 52-year-old man, a serving Bradford councillor, had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.

Police said: “The man is believed to have first been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to Manse Street where emergency services attended. He was taken to hospital where his condition is described as serious but not life-threatening.”

West Yorkshire police said there was nothing to suggest the incident was politically motivated, although the investigation was at an early stage.

Police cordons were in place on Manse Street, Leeds Road and Thornbury Avenue while inquiries are carried out.

Jim McMahon, the MP for Oldham West, described the attack as “horrific” and said: “Our thoughts are with [Ali], his family, councillors in Bradford and, of course, our members of parliament too.

“Our thoughts are very much with you all at this time.”

Imran Hussain, the MP for Bradford East, said: “This horrific attack is deeply disturbing. My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family.

“No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community. I am receiving regular updates from the police as they deal with this extremely serious incident, and I understand a suspect is in police custody.”

Sharon Taylor, a local government minister, named Ali in the House of Lords. Lady Taylor said: “I am afraid I have to mention a very tragic incident that’s occurred in Bradford … where an independent councillor who was out canvassing has been stabbed.

“I would want to send the wishes, that I’m sure noble lords would agree, of the whole house to councillor Ibrar Ali for a speedy recovery, and our thoughts are with all of those in Bradford who are affected by this awful incident.”

Adam, who works in the area and did not want to give his surname, said: “I know the councillor on a personal level and it’s shocking. I just know he’s a very kind, warm-hearted man whose goal is to serve, his life is to help out everyone.

“He just wants everyone to succeed. He definitely didn’t deserve what’s happened.

“The world’s not a nice place.”

Chris Herd, the lord mayor of Bradford, said: “It is deeply distressing that this incident has occurred.

“Councillors work tirelessly on behalf of residents across the district and should be able to carry out their duties safely.

“We will continue to work closely with our colleagues at West Yorkshire police as they investigate this matter and seek to bring those responsible to justice, and would like to thank those who provided aid and support at the time.”

Press Association contributed to this report

output.progress: Police have cordoned off three streets and are investigating, with the lord mayor saying the council will help bring those responsible to justice.

output.headline: Prosecutors set out case against man accused of killing British woman
output.bodyHtml:
Prosecutors in Ocala, Florida, have been setting out an extraordinary criminal case against Dwain C Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver accused of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, of Portsmouth, England.

Hall has pleaded not guilty to the charges, which allege that he lured Exelby to the US before killing her in October last year and burying her body in a shallow grave in Marion Oaks.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. After Hall’s arrest in November 2025, investigators said Exelby had travelled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life, and prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts, and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported.

Authorities have said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.

After Exelby travelled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from Gainesville airport in central Florida and drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

In a text message from Exelby’s phone to a friend, she said she felt scared and trapped, according to the arrest affidavit. “I’m sorry, he keeps taking my phone, he doesn’t trust me with it,” she wrote. “He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him.”

In opening statements this week, assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said Exelby’s parents struggled with mental illness and addiction and that their daughter had also struggled with mental illness and twice attempted suicide.

She had visited a website depicting graphic sexual abuse of women, where Hall was among several men who contacted her.

Berndt said in court that Exelby “was trying to find some substitute” to the self-harm. “Unfortunately, she found another outlet.” Berndt said Exelby was “trying to find someone who would kill her”.

“Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible,” Berndt added.

After she disappeared from her home, a former boyfriend, Stevie Hunt, contacted the authorities, the court heard.

In court, Hunt described Exelby as a kind, beautiful and loving woman, while her sister talked about their difficult childhood. Hunt told the court that Exelby experienced mood swings that sometimes lasted for days and had been in therapy for more than a decade.

Hall has denied killing Exelby but acknowledged in a police interview that he had been in contact with her and that the two had been intimate. Evidence linking Hall to Exelby’s death includes a shovel with Exelby’s blood on it, cellphone data, and a knife recovered from a friend of the defendant.

Prosecutors have said jurors will be shown photographs and surveillance video of Hall making purchases including rope, a shovel, deodorant and other items at a local Walmart store.

Hall’s defense attorney Junior Barrett said in opening statements that his client was not a murderer and asked jurors to carefully consider the facts, witness testimony and circumstances of the case.

“We believe that when you listen to all the facts and evidence in this case, you will arrive at the decision that Dwain Hall did not murder,” Barrett said.

The case continues.

output.headline: Spacecraft reaches Mercury, nears only the second orbit in history
output.bodyHtml:
After a voyage of more than eight years and 6bn miles, a joint European-Japanese space mission has reached Mercury and is preparing to swing into orbit around the tiny, barely explored world.

The BepiColombo mission is poised to become only the second in history to circle the first rock from the sun and the smallest planet in the solar system, when flight controllers fire the spacecraft’s thrusters on Saturday and send it into orbit.

For researchers, the €1.6bn (£1.4bn) mission is the best hope yet of understanding how Mercury formed so close to the sun, why it has a magnetic field and what makes up the frozen ice that lurks in the planet’s permanently shadowed craters.

‘We’re very excited, it’s been a long wait,’ said Prof Emma Bunce at the University of Leicester, who has worked on the project for 20 years.

Getting to Mercury poses unusual difficulties. Because the planet is near the centre of the solar system, spacecraft accelerate under the sun’s gravity and must spend much of their time braking to avoid shooting straight past. ‘It’s a very complex and challenging mission,’ said Bunce, the principal investigator on an instrument called the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer, or MIXS, which will analyse the geochemical composition of the planet’s surface.

It will be some months before scientists can start observing Mercury. In early December, the spacecraft will separate into two orbiters, one European, the other Japanese, which will manoeuvre to different polar orbits around the planet. Science operations are due to start in April next year.

The European probe, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter or MPO, will map the planet’s surface and composition at high resolution, and study Mercury’s interior to shed light on its unusually large core. Its Japanese partner will measure the planet’s magnetic field and its sodium exosphere, the extremely thin layer of gas and atoms that surrounds the planet. Mercury is only 50 per cent larger than the moon but has four times its mass. One question the mission will explore is why the rock is so dense.

Prof Geraint Jones, the lead project scientist on BepiColombo at the European Space Agency, said anticipation of the scientific results had kept everyone enthused during the spacecraft’s eight-year journey.

‘We’re expecting to learn a huge amount, bringing more powerful instruments on two spacecraft to study all aspects of the planet – its interior, surface, and the space around it,’ he said.

Mercury is a planet of extremes. The tiny world takes 58 Earth days to rotate on its axis, meaning any given spot on the surface can experience daylight for three months and then night-time for three months. It is little more than a third of Earth’s distance from the sun, at only 36m miles. In the day, ground temperatures reach 450C while at night they drop to -180C.

Jones said: ‘As well as cameras covering a wide range of wavelengths to study the surface, we’ll be “tasting” the gases around the planet, sensing the magnetic field, probing the interior with ultrasensitive instruments, and mapping the shape of the whole planet with a laser.’

The spacecraft are expected to orbit Mercury for about three years, after which they will run out of fuel, lose altitude and ultimately slam into the surface. ‘Sadly, they are not coming back,’ said Bunce.
